title: Understanding Deep Learning
byline: Simon J. D. Prince · draft of January 23, 2023 (MIT Press)
note: This draft predates the published edition, so its numbering differs from the edition on the author’s site. Page numbers are PDF pages (printed page = PDF page − 13). Summaries are in our own words; the text stays in the PDF.
summary: Prince builds deep learning from one idea outward: a network is a parameterized family of functions, and training picks one member of that family. With ReLU activations every network is piecewise linear, so the early chapters can draw exactly what shallow and deep networks compute: linear regions, joints and folds of input space. Losses then come from maximum likelihood, fitting from gradient methods, and generalization from bias, variance and double descent. The middle of the book adds the architectures that share parameters or route information: convolutions, residual connections, transformers and graph networks. The last part covers four families of generative models (GANs, normalizing flows, VAEs, diffusion), each framed by what it can and cannot do: sample, evaluate likelihood, or both.

chapters.title: 1. Introduction
chapters.summary: What deep learning is, the three settings it is used in, and how the book is organized. It closes with an unusually direct section on the ethics of AI.

sections.title: 1.1 Supervised learning
sections.summary: Supervised learning maps inputs to outputs: regression predicts numbers, classification predicts categories, and structured outputs (text, images, segmentations) are the hard case. Deep networks are introduced as one very flexible family of such mappings.

sections.title: 1.2 Unsupervised learning
sections.summary: Unsupervised learning works without labels. Generative models learn to produce new examples like the data, and latent variables give a compact explanation of what varies between examples.

sections.title: 1.3 Reinforcement learning
sections.summary: Shows how latent variables also help supervised problems with structured outputs, then introduces reinforcement learning: an agent acts, the world changes, rewards arrive late. Temporal credit assignment and the explore/exploit trade-off are the core difficulties.

sections.title: 1.4 Structure of book
sections.summary: Two worked RL examples (robot locomotion, chess), then the book's roadmap: supervised pipeline first, then specialized architectures, then generative models.

sections.title: 1.5 Ethics
sections.summary: Five concerns are named: bias and fairness, explainability, weaponization, concentration of power, and existential risk. The author argues researchers carry real responsibility for how the technology is used.

sections.title: 1.6 Other books
sections.summary: Continues the ethics discussion (accountability, who funds AI, whether harm can be controlled) and lists complementary books.

sections.title: 1.7 How to read this book
sections.summary: How each chapter is laid out (main text, notes, problems) and where the background maths lives.

chapters.title: 2. Supervised learning
chapters.summary: The whole supervised pipeline on the smallest possible example: a straight line fitted to points.

sections.title: 2.1 Supervised learning overview
sections.summary: A model is an equation with parameters; inference runs it, training searches for parameter values that make predictions match a training set.

sections.title: 2.2 Linear regression example
sections.summary: One input, one output, two parameters. A least-squares loss scores each line, and the loss over all parameter values forms a surface that training walks down.

sections.title: 2.3 Summary
sections.summary: Training descends the loss surface by gradient; testing on held-out data shows whether the fit generalizes. Too simple a model underfits, too flexible a model overfits.

chapters.title: 3. Shallow neural networks
chapters.summary: Networks with one hidden layer, analyzed geometrically. With ReLU they produce piecewise-linear functions, and enough hidden units can approximate anything.

sections.title: 3.1 Neural network example
sections.summary: A 1D network with three hidden units: three linear functions, each clipped by a ReLU, then summed with weights. The result is piecewise linear with joints where units switch on or off.

sections.title: 3.2 Universal approximation theorem
sections.summary: With D hidden units a 1D network has at most D+1 linear regions, and with enough units it can approximate any continuous function on a bounded interval.

sections.title: 3.3 Multivariate inputs and outputs
sections.summary: More outputs share the same joints; more inputs turn the joints into lines or hyperplanes that divide input space into convex polygonal regions.

sections.title: 3.4 Shallow neural networks: general case
sections.summary: The general equation for a shallow network with any number of inputs, hidden units and outputs. The count of linear regions grows fast with input dimension.

sections.title: 3.5 Terminology
sections.summary: Vocabulary: layers, hidden units (neurons), pre-activations and activations, MLP, fully connected.

sections.title: 3.6 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes on the history and on other activation functions (sigmoid, tanh, leaky ReLU, GELU, Swish and others).

chapters.title: 4. Deep neural networks
chapters.summary: Why depth helps: composing networks folds input space, so deep networks create far more linear regions per parameter than shallow ones.

sections.title: 4.1 Composing neural networks
sections.summary: Feeding one shallow network into another repeats the second network's function on each piece of the first's output.

sections.title: 4.2 From composing networks to deep networks
sections.summary: Composition can be read as folding: the first network maps several input ranges onto the same output range, and the second network's function is applied to all of them at once. The composed network is a special case of a two-layer network.

sections.title: 4.3 Deep neural networks
sections.summary: The general two-hidden-layer network, and hyperparameters (depth and width) as choices about model capacity.

sections.title: 4.4 Matrix notation
sections.summary: Writing a deep network as alternating weight matrices, bias vectors and activations, layer by layer.

sections.title: 4.5 Shallow vs. deep neural networks
sections.summary: Shallow and deep networks can both approximate anything, but deep ones get many more regions per parameter, some functions need exponentially many shallow units, and deep networks handle large structured inputs better. Why they also train and generalize well is left open.

sections.title: 4.6 Summary
sections.summary: Recap of folding, depth efficiency and the open questions.

chapters.title: 5. Loss functions
chapters.summary: Where loss functions come from: the network predicts the parameters of a probability distribution over outputs, and training maximizes the likelihood of the data.

sections.title: 5.1 Maximum likelihood
sections.summary: The model outputs distribution parameters; maximum likelihood picks parameters that make the observed outputs probable, and taking logs turns the product over examples into a sum.

sections.title: 5.2 Recipe for constructing loss functions
sections.summary: The recipe: choose a distribution suited to the output domain, have the network predict its parameters, minimize negative log-likelihood. Inference returns the most probable output.

sections.title: 5.3 Example 1: univariate regression
sections.summary: Assuming normally distributed outputs and predicting only the mean gives least squares. Predicting the variance too gives uncertainty estimates, and making the variance depend on the input gives heteroscedastic regression.

sections.title: 5.4 Example 2: binary classification
sections.summary: A Bernoulli output passed through a logistic sigmoid gives the binary cross-entropy loss.

sections.title: 5.5 Example 3: multiclass classification
sections.summary: A categorical distribution with a softmax gives the multiclass cross-entropy loss.

sections.title: 5.6 Multiple outputs
sections.summary: Several outputs are usually treated as independent, so their losses add. A table maps output types (circular, counts, rankings and others) to suitable distributions.

sections.title: 5.7 Cross-entropy loss
sections.summary: Cross-entropy is the KL divergence between the empirical data distribution and the model, minus a constant, so it is the same objective as negative log-likelihood.

sections.title: 5.8 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes on robust losses, mixtures of Gaussians for multimodal outputs, and other distributions.

chapters.title: 6. Fitting models
chapters.summary: How parameters are actually found: gradient descent and the stochastic, momentum-based and adaptive refinements used in practice.

sections.title: 6.1 Gradient descent
sections.summary: Gradient descent steps against the gradient. Linear regression has a convex loss with one minimum; the nonlinear Gabor model shows a loss surface with many.

sections.title: 6.2 Stochastic gradient descent
sections.summary: Local minima and saddle points trap plain gradient descent. Stochastic gradient descent uses random batches and epochs, so each step sees a slightly different loss surface.

sections.title: 6.3 Momentum
sections.summary: SGD's noise helps escape bad regions and is cheap per step. Momentum averages past gradients to smooth the path; Nesterov momentum measures the gradient after the momentum step.

sections.title: 6.4 Adam
sections.summary: Adam normalizes each parameter's step by a running estimate of its gradient magnitude, so steep and shallow directions move at similar rates. Bias corrections fix the early estimates.

sections.title: 6.5 Training algorithm hyperparameters
sections.summary: Learning rate, batch size, schedule and momentum are hyperparameters of training, usually tuned by trial.

sections.title: 6.6 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes on convexity, line search, learning-rate schedules and other optimizers.

chapters.title: 7. Gradients and initialization
chapters.summary: Two problems specific to neural networks: computing gradients for every parameter efficiently, and initializing so that signals neither explode nor vanish.

sections.title: 7.1 Problem definitions
sections.summary: The setup: total loss is a sum over examples, and training needs its derivative for every weight and bias at every step.

sections.title: 7.2 Computing derivatives
sections.summary: Backpropagation runs a forward pass storing activations, then a backward pass applying the chain rule layer by layer. It is a special case of reverse-mode algorithmic differentiation, which frameworks automate.

sections.title: 7.3 Parameter initialization
sections.summary: Backprop extends to any computational graph and works on batches as tensors. For initialization, the variance of activations and gradients should stay constant across layers; for ReLU this gives He initialization.

sections.title: 7.4 Example training code
sections.summary: When adjacent layers differ in width, averaging the two sizes is a compromise. A short PyTorch listing shows the whole training loop so far.

sections.title: 7.5 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes on the history of backprop and on initialization schemes.

chapters.title: 8. Measuring performance
chapters.summary: How to measure and explain test error, from the classical bias-variance trade-off to double descent in over-parameterized models.

sections.title: 8.1 Training a simple model
sections.summary: A network trained on the MNIST-1D toy dataset reaches zero training error but much higher test error.

sections.title: 8.2 Sources of error
sections.summary: Test error splits into noise (irreducible), bias (the model family can't represent the truth) and variance (the fit depends on which training sample you drew).

sections.title: 8.3 Reducing error
sections.summary: More data reduces variance; more capacity reduces bias but raises variance. Classically the best model sits at a trade-off point.

sections.title: 8.4 Double descent
sections.summary: Past the point where the model can memorize the training data, test error falls again: double descent. In this regime the question becomes why training picks smooth solutions among many that fit.

sections.title: 8.5 Choosing hyperparameters
sections.summary: Hyperparameters are tuned on a separate validation set, never the test set, usually by random or Bayesian search.

sections.title: 8.6 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes including why high-dimensional spaces behave counterintuitively.

chapters.title: 9. Regularization
chapters.summary: Techniques that shrink the gap between training and test performance, from explicit penalty terms to the implicit biases of SGD and a long list of heuristics.

sections.title: 9.1 Explicit regularization
sections.summary: Adding a penalty term to the loss, read as a prior over parameters; L2 regularization (weight decay) favors small weights and smoother functions.

sections.title: 9.2 Implicit regularization
sections.summary: Finite-step gradient descent behaves like continuous descent on a modified loss that penalizes steep gradients. SGD adds a term favoring places where batches agree, one reason larger learning rates and smaller batches can generalize better.

sections.title: 9.3 Heuristics to improve performance
sections.summary: Early stopping, ensembling and bagging, dropout, adding noise, Bayesian inference, transfer and multi-task learning, self-supervised pretraining and data augmentation, each explained by how it improves generalization.

sections.title: 9.4 Summary
sections.summary: The methods sorted by mechanism: smoother functions, more data, better initialization, or averaging. Notes on sharp versus flat minima.

chapters.title: 10. Convolutional networks
chapters.summary: Convolutional layers for grid data: weight sharing builds in translation equivariance, which cuts parameters and improves generalization.

sections.title: 10.1 Invariance and equivariance
sections.summary: Images are high-dimensional, nearby pixels are related, and meaning shouldn't change under translation. Equivariance and invariance make the last point precise.

sections.title: 10.2 Convolutional networks for 1D inputs
sections.summary: 1D convolution, padding, stride, kernel size and dilation; channels and growing receptive fields; on MNIST-1D a convolutional network beats a fully connected one with far fewer parameters.

sections.title: 10.3 Convolutional networks for 2D inputs
sections.summary: The same machinery in two dimensions, with kernels spanning all input channels.

sections.title: 10.4 Downsampling and upsampling
sections.summary: Downsampling (subsampling, max and mean pooling, strided convolution), upsampling (duplication, max-unpooling, transposed convolution) and 1×1 convolutions to change channel counts.

sections.title: 10.5 Applications
sections.summary: Image classification (AlexNet, VGG on ImageNet), object detection (YOLO) and semantic segmentation with an encoder–decoder network.

sections.title: 10.6 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes on the history of CNNs and the steady ImageNet gains.

chapters.title: 11. Residual networks
chapters.summary: Residual connections make very deep networks trainable; batch normalization keeps their activations in check.

sections.title: 11.1 Sequential processing
sections.summary: Simply stacking more layers made results worse. Shattered gradients, where small parameter changes alter the output unpredictably, are one explanation.

sections.title: 11.2 Residual connections and residual blocks
sections.summary: Each block adds a change to its input rather than replacing it, so the network unrolls into many paths of different lengths. Order of operations inside a block matters.

sections.title: 11.3 Exploding gradients in residual networks
sections.summary: In residual networks the variance of activations grows with each block at initialization, even with He initialization.

sections.title: 11.4 Batch normalization
sections.summary: Batch normalization rescales each activation using batch statistics, with learned offset and scale. It stabilizes forward signals, allows higher learning rates and adds a little regularizing noise.

sections.title: 11.5 Common residual architectures
sections.summary: ResNet blocks and bottlenecks, DenseNet's concatenation of earlier layers, and U-Nets and stacked hourglass networks for dense prediction.

sections.title: 11.6 Why do nets with residual connections perform so well?
sections.summary: Residual nets behave partly like ensembles of shallower paths, and their loss surfaces are smoother around minima.

sections.title: 11.7 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes on other normalization schemes (layer, instance, group norm) and on why residual connections work.

chapters.title: 12. Transformers
chapters.summary: Transformers: self-attention lets every token weigh every other, with parameters shared across positions. Covers the architecture and its main uses in language and vision.

sections.title: 12.1 Processing text data
sections.summary: Text is long, variable in length and ambiguous, so a network needs shared parameters and connections whose strength depends on the content.

sections.title: 12.2 Dot-product self-attention
sections.summary: Each output is a weighted sum of value vectors; the weights come from softmaxed dot products between queries and keys, all computed by shared linear maps. In matrix form this is one compact expression.

sections.title: 12.3 Extensions to dot-product self-attention
sections.summary: Position encodings break the permutation symmetry, scaling the dot products keeps softmax well behaved, and multiple heads attend in parallel.

sections.title: 12.4 Transformer layers
sections.summary: A transformer layer: multi-head attention and a per-token MLP, each wrapped in a residual connection, with LayerNorm.

sections.title: 12.5 Transformers for natural language processing
sections.summary: The NLP pipeline: sub-word tokenization (byte-pair encoding), learned embeddings, then a stack of layers in one of three forms: encoder, decoder or encoder-decoder.

sections.title: 12.6 Encoder model example: BERT
sections.summary: BERT as the encoder example: pretraining by predicting masked tokens, then fine-tuning for classification or tagging.

sections.title: 12.7 Decoder model example: GPT3
sections.summary: GPT-3 as the decoder example: next-token prediction with masked attention, autoregressive generation, and few-shot learning from prompts.

sections.title: 12.8 Encoder-decoder model example: machine translation
sections.summary: Machine translation as the encoder-decoder example, with cross-attention from target to source.

sections.title: 12.9 Transformers for long sequences
sections.summary: Attention cost grows quadratically with length; sparse and local interaction patterns cut the cost.

sections.title: 12.10 Transformers for images
sections.summary: ImageGPT models pixels autoregressively; ViT treats image patches as tokens; multi-scale transformers like SWIN reintroduce hierarchy.

sections.title: 12.11 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes on RNNs as the predecessor and on efficient-attention variants.

chapters.title: 13. Graph neural networks
chapters.summary: Graph neural networks: layers that must be equivariant to node order, and the extra problems of huge or single graphs.

sections.title: 13.1 What is a graph?
sections.summary: Graphs model roads, molecules, circuits and social networks; they can be directed, weighted, hierarchical and more.

sections.title: 13.2 Graph representation
sections.summary: A graph is stored as an adjacency matrix plus node and edge embeddings. Powers of the adjacency matrix count walks.

sections.title: 13.3 Graph neural networks, tasks, and loss functions
sections.summary: Node numbering is arbitrary, so a layer must give the same answer under any permutation of the nodes.

sections.title: 13.4 Tasks and loss functions
sections.summary: Graph-level, node-level and edge-prediction tasks, each with its loss.

sections.title: 13.5 Graph convolutional networks
sections.summary: A graph convolutional layer aggregates neighbors' embeddings (multiplying by the adjacency matrix plus identity) and shares weights across the graph.

sections.title: 13.6 Example: graph classification
sections.summary: Classifying molecules as toxic or not; batches are built by treating many graphs as one disconnected graph.

sections.title: 13.7 Inductive vs. transductive models
sections.summary: Inductive models learn a rule for new graphs; transductive models label the unlabeled nodes of one graph seen during training.

sections.title: 13.8 Transductive learning example: node classification
sections.summary: Node classification on one huge graph needs batching via neighborhood sampling or graph partitioning, because receptive fields grow with depth.

sections.title: 13.9 Layers for graph convolutional networks
sections.summary: Design choices inside a layer: treating the node differently from its neighbors, residual connections, mean or Kipf-normalized aggregation, max pooling, and graph attention.

sections.title: 13.10 Edge graphs
sections.summary: Turning edges into nodes lets the same machinery work on edge embeddings.

sections.title: 13.11 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes on spectral methods, expressiveness and the Weisfeiler–Lehman test.

chapters.title: 14. Unsupervised learning
chapters.summary: A short map of unsupervised learning that frames the next four chapters.

sections.title: 14.1 Taxonomy of unsupervised learning models
sections.summary: Models learned without labels; generative models can sample, probabilistic ones also assign likelihoods, latent-variable models map a simple latent space to data.

sections.title: 14.2 What makes a good generative model?
sections.summary: Desired properties: efficient sampling, high quality, coverage of the data, a well-behaved latent space and the ability to evaluate probability. No family has all of them.

sections.title: 14.3 Quantifying performance
sections.summary: Ways to score generative models: test likelihood, Inception score, FID, and manifold-based precision and recall.

sections.title: 14.4 Summary
sections.summary: Recap of the taxonomy and what each later chapter's model can do.

chapters.title: 15. Generative Adversarial Networks
chapters.summary: GANs generate samples by fooling a discriminator. Much of the chapter is about why training is unstable and how to fix it.

sections.title: 15.1 Discrimination as a signal
sections.summary: A generator maps noise to samples and a discriminator learns to tell them from real data; the two play a minimax game. DCGAN made it work for images, but training is hard.

sections.title: 15.2 Improving stability
sections.summary: Mode dropping and collapse; the original loss gives vanishing gradients when the discriminator wins. The Wasserstein distance, from optimal transport, gives a smoother signal and a more stable loss.

sections.title: 15.3 Improving quality
sections.summary: Progressive growing, minibatch discrimination and truncation of the latent distribution improve image quality and diversity.

sections.title: 15.4 Conditional generation
sections.summary: Conditional GANs and auxiliary-classifier GANs generate samples with chosen attributes.

sections.title: 15.5 Image translation
sections.summary: InfoGAN discovers interpretable attributes on its own; Pix2Pix and CycleGAN translate images between styles, with and without paired examples.

sections.title: 15.6 StyleGAN
sections.summary: StyleGAN injects style vectors and noise at several scales, separating coarse and fine variation.

sections.title: 15.7 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes on the large GAN literature and evaluation.

chapters.title: 16. Normalizing flows
chapters.summary: Normalizing flows transform a simple distribution through invertible layers, so they can both sample and compute exact likelihoods.

sections.title: 16.1 1D Normalizing flows example
sections.summary: A 1D example: probability changes by the slope of the mapping, so an invertible function gives a density you can evaluate in either direction.

sections.title: 16.2 General case
sections.summary: In many dimensions the scaling factor is the Jacobian determinant. A deep flow is a stack of invertible layers trained by maximum likelihood.

sections.title: 16.3 Invertible network layers
sections.summary: Layers must be expressive, invertible and have cheap Jacobians. Linear, elementwise, coupling, autoregressive and inverse-autoregressive flows, then residual flows (iRevNet, iResNet).

sections.title: 16.4 Multi-scale flows
sections.summary: Multi-scale flows set some latent dimensions aside early to save computation.

sections.title: 16.5 Applications
sections.summary: Density modeling and image synthesis (GLOW), and using a flow to approximate another density model.

sections.title: 16.6 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes and the open question of why flow samples trail GANs and diffusion.

chapters.title: 17. Variational autoencoders
chapters.summary: VAEs train a nonlinear latent-variable model by maximizing a lower bound on likelihood, using an encoder to approximate the posterior.

sections.title: 17.1 Latent variable models
sections.summary: The data distribution is modeled by marginalizing over a hidden variable.

sections.title: 17.2 Nonlinear latent variable model
sections.summary: A mixture of Gaussians as the simple case; then a deep network maps a continuous latent to the data mean, and new samples come from ancestral sampling.

sections.title: 17.3 Training
sections.summary: The likelihood integral is intractable, so Jensen's inequality gives the evidence lower bound (ELBO).

sections.title: 17.4 ELBO properties
sections.summary: The bound is tight when the auxiliary distribution equals the posterior; it can be read as reconstruction quality minus distance to the prior.

sections.title: 17.5 Variational approximation
sections.summary: Choose a simple (Gaussian) auxiliary distribution and fit it to the true posterior.

sections.title: 17.6 The variational autoencoder
sections.summary: The VAE: an encoder predicts the approximate posterior for each example, and a decoder reconstructs the data from samples.

sections.title: 17.7 The reparameterization trick
sections.summary: The reparameterization trick moves randomness into an input so gradients flow through the sampling step.

sections.title: 17.8 Applications
sections.summary: Estimating sample probability by importance sampling, generation, resynthesis and disentangled latent spaces.

sections.title: 17.9 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes on β-VAE, other variants and the link to expectation maximization.

chapters.title: 18. Diffusion models
chapters.summary: Diffusion models add noise in many small steps and learn to undo them. The ELBO reduces to a simple noise-prediction loss.

sections.title: 18.1 Overview
sections.summary: Like flows the latent has the data's size; like VAEs training uses a lower bound. The encoder is fixed noise addition.

sections.title: 18.2 Encoder (forward process)
sections.summary: The forward process blends data with Gaussian noise under a schedule. Closed-form diffusion kernels and conditional distributions make every step's distribution computable.

sections.title: 18.3 Decoder model (reverse process)
sections.summary: The decoder approximates each reverse step with a Gaussian whose mean a network predicts.

sections.title: 18.4 Training
sections.summary: The ELBO simplifies to a sum of KL terms between Gaussians, giving a least-squares loss and a simple training procedure.

sections.title: 18.5 Reparameterization of loss function
sections.summary: Reparameterizing so the network predicts the added noise gives the simplest, best-performing loss.

sections.title: 18.6 Implementation
sections.summary: Image diffusion with U-Nets, faster sampling (DDIM and others), classifier and classifier-free guidance, and cascaded text-to-image generation.

sections.title: 18.7 Summary
sections.summary: Recap, then notes on score matching and related views.
